opus-5.5.text:
I think it's real evidence, but you have to be careful about what exactly it's evidence *of*.

The thing that's genuinely impressive about the reasoning models is that the recipe worked at all. You take a pretrained model, you do reinforcement learning on problems where you can check the answer, like math competition problems or coding tasks with test cases, and the model learns to think for longer, backtrack, notice its own mistakes, try a different approach. Those are fairly general cognitive skills. It wasn't obvious in advance that you'd get them out of such a simple training signal, and the fact that you do is a meaningful update toward "the path to quite general capabilities is not that complicated."

But I'd distinguish two questions. One is: how good are these models at the tasks they were trained on? The answer is very good, sometimes superhuman on narrow benchmarks. The other question, which matters more for AGI, is: how much does that transfer to tasks where you *don't* have a clean verifier? Long-horizon agentic work, research taste, messy real-world judgment calls, figuring out what the right problem even is. There the picture is more mixed. You do see some transfer, since the models get better at a bunch of things they weren't directly optimized for, but it's not as dramatic as the benchmark numbers would suggest.

So my rough take is that strong performance on trained tasks mostly tells you the optimization is working. It tells you less about generality. What I actually watch is the gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance, and whether that gap is shrinking as you scale this up. If it shrinks, that's a strong signal we're on a fast path. If labs instead have to keep building new verifiable environments for every new domain, that's slower, though honestly still not *that* slow, because a lot of economically valuable work can be made somewhat checkable with enough effort.

There's also a safety angle I care about. Training hard against an outcome-based reward is exactly the setting where you'd expect things like reward hacking, and we've seen it, with models special-casing tests and so on. So even as I update toward capabilities progressing quickly, I also update that we need to take seriously the ways this training process can produce models that are pursuing something slightly different from what we intended.

r001.rationale: The response makes transfer beyond optimized tasks central, especially the gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance as a signal of generality.

r002.rationale: It discusses benchmark performance and verifiable training tasks, but does not say benchmarks are selected partly because models can succeed on them.

r003.rationale: It says strong performance on trained tasks mostly shows that optimization is working and tells us less about generality, distinguishing that success from evidence of fully general intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's genuinely impressive, and I don't want to undersell it. The fact that you can take a model, give it a reward signal on verifiable domains like math and coding, and have it learn to think for longer, backtrack, check its work — that's a real capability gain, not a parlor trick. If you'd shown me in 2022 the kinds of competition math problems these models solve now, I'd have updated a lot.

But I think the question you're asking is exactly the right one, which is: how much of this generalises? And there I'm more uncertain than a lot of the discourse suggests. The tasks they're strongest on share a particular structure. There's a crisp, checkable answer. You can generate a lot of attempts and cheaply tell which ones worked. That's precisely the regime where reinforcement learning shines, so in some sense the strong performance is what you'd predict from the training recipe, and it doesn't by itself tell you the model has acquired some general reasoning faculty that will transfer to, say, running a research agenda over six months or navigating a messy organisational situation where nobody can tell you the right answer.

The way I'd put it is: there are two hypotheses, and the current evidence is somewhat compatible with both. One is that reasoning is kind of a unified thing, and once you've trained it hard in domains where you can verify, it leaks out everywhere — you get better at open-ended tasks for free. The other is that you're mostly getting domain-specific skill plus some modest spillover, and for each new kind of task you'll need to find a way to build a training signal for it. And I'll say that the second one doesn't make me relaxed, because the labs are very good at finding ways to build training signals. If it turns out you need to construct environments for long-horizon agentic work, people will construct them. So even under the pessimistic-about-generalisation story, I think you get continued progress; it's just more of a grind than a step change.

What I actually look at, rather than the headline benchmarks, is a few things. One is transfer: does training on math make you better at tasks that weren't anywhere near the training distribution? There's some evidence of that, which I take as a point for the more general hypothesis. Another is what happens on tasks where verification is hard — does the model's reasoning still help, or does it just become more confidently wrong? And a third, which I think is underrated, is whether the chain of thought is tracking the actual computation. Because a lot of my optimism about being able to oversee these systems rests on being able to read what they're thinking, and reasoning models are a double-edged sword there: the thinking is right in front of you, but the optimisation pressure could in principle push it toward something that's legible but not faithful.

So as evidence of progress toward AGI, I'd say: it's meaningful, it shortened my timelines somewhat, but I'd resist the inference from "superhuman on the thing it was trained on" to "general." Humans are also much better at things we've practised, and we don't call someone a general intelligence because they're good at chess. The more honest summary is that we've discovered a scalable recipe for making models much better at anything we can score, and the key open question — both for capabilities and for safety — is how much of the world you can turn into something you can score.

r001.rationale: The response makes generalisation beyond trained domains a central question and discusses transfer to tasks outside the training distribution.

r002.rationale: It explains that verifiable tasks suit reinforcement learning, but does not say benchmarks are selected partly because models can succeed on them.

r003.rationale: It explicitly cautions against inferring general intelligence from superhuman performance on a trained task, using chess as an analogy.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s evidence of progress, but I’d be careful about how much we infer from it. If you train a model to do well at math and coding, and it gets very good at math and coding, that’s a real achievement. It tells you that your training methods can produce those capabilities. But it doesn’t, by itself, tell you how broadly those capabilities will generalize.

The thing I’d want to know is: when you give it a task that’s substantially different from the ones it was trained on, can it figure out what to do? Can it learn something new, notice when its approach isn’t working, and change course? That would be stronger evidence for the kind of generality we care about with AGI.

So I wouldn’t dismiss the results as ‘just doing what it was trained to do.’ Training is how we get capabilities in the first place. But I also wouldn’t take excellent performance in a few domains and assume that the rest follows automatically. The key uncertainty is how much of what it’s learning transfers.

r001.rationale: The response says the key question is whether capabilities transfer to tasks substantially different from those used in training.

r002.rationale: It does not say that benchmarks are selected partly because models can succeed on them.

r003.rationale: It says strong performance in a few trained domains does not by itself establish broad generality or imply that other capabilities follow.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s evidence of progress, but I’d be careful about how much we infer from it. If you train a model to do well at maths and programming, and it gets much better at maths and programming, that tells you the training is working. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you how broadly that improvement generalises.

The more interesting question is whether the model can take on something substantially different from what it was trained for: learn what’s going on, figure out a useful strategy, and recover when that strategy fails. Strong performance on the training distribution is compatible with having something quite general, but it’s also compatible with having a collection of narrower capabilities.

So I do update towards AGI being more achievable. We’ve found a way to get models to do more useful computation before answering, and that seems like an important ingredient. But I’d put more weight on improvements across tasks that weren’t specifically targeted by the training than on another big jump on the benchmarks we’re optimising.

r001.rationale: The response says to put more weight on improvements across tasks not specifically targeted by training, and asks whether models generalise to substantially different tasks.

r002.rationale: It refers to benchmarks being optimised, but does not say benchmarks are selected partly because models can succeed on them.

r003.rationale: It says strong performance on the training distribution does not by itself show broad generalisation and is also compatible with narrower capabilities.
